title: Die Alte im Wald
titleEn: The Old Woman in the Forest
part: The Old Woman in the Forest
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 123. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 123 follows a servant girl who is the sole survivor when robbers ambush her master's carriage in the deep forest, and who is fed, housed and clothed there by a dove that keeps bringing her golden keys to a hollow tree. Sent on one last errand — to slip past an old woman and pick the plainest ring from a table heaped with glittering ones — she passes where greed would have failed, and the tree beside her turns out to be an enchanted man. It is a quiet tale of patience rewarded, without the violence some of its neighbors carry.

sentences.t: Es fuhr einmal ein armes Dienstmädchen mit seiner Herrschaft durch einen großen Wald, und als sie mitten darin waren, kamen Räuber aus dem Dickicht hervor und ermordeten wen sie fanden.
sentences.l: There drove once a poor serving-girl with her master’s household through a great forest, and when they were in the middle of it, robbers came forth out of the thicket and murdered whom they found.
sentences.i: A poor serving-girl was once travelling with the household she served through a great forest, and when they were in the midst of it, robbers came out of the thicket and murdered everyone they found.
sentences.n: “Herrschaft” is the master and mistress a servant belongs to — the family she travels with. Note that the girl is “das Mädchen,” a neuter noun, so the German calls her “es” and “ihm” all through this tale; the English says “she” and “her.” “ermordeten wen sie fanden” — the relative pronoun stands with nothing before it: murdered whomever they found.

sentences.t: Da kamen alle mit einander um bis auf das Mädchen, das war in der Angst aus dem Wagen gesprungen und hatte sich hinter einen Baum verborgen.
sentences.l: Then all perished with one another except for the girl; she had in her fear sprung out of the carriage and had hidden herself behind a tree.
sentences.i: So all of them perished together but the girl; in her terror she had jumped from the carriage and hidden behind a tree.
sentences.n: “umkommen” — to perish, with the particle um thrown to the end. “bis auf” means “except for,” not “up to.” “das war … gesprungen”: the demonstrative das picks the girl up again where English begins a new sentence with “she.”

sentences.t: Wie die Räuber mit ihrer Beute fort waren, trat es herbei und sah das große Unglück.
sentences.l: When the robbers were away with their booty, she stepped near and saw the great misfortune.
sentences.i: When the robbers had gone off with their plunder, she came out and saw the great calamity.
sentences.n: “es” is the girl again — the neuter pronoun follows the neuter noun Mädchen, not the person. “herbeitreten,” to step up close, with herbei carrying the direction “over here.”

sentences.t: Da fieng es an bitterlich zu weinen und sagte „was soll ich armes Mädchen nun anfangen, ich weiß mich nicht aus dem Wald heraus zu finden, keine Menschenseele wohnt darin, so muß ich gewiß verhungern.“
sentences.l: Then she began bitterly to weep and said “what shall I poor girl now begin, I do not know how to find my way out of the forest, no human soul lives in it, so I must surely starve.”
sentences.i: Then she began to weep bitterly and said: “What am I, poor girl, to do now? I cannot find my way out of the forest, not a soul lives in it, and so I must surely starve to death.”
sentences.n: “fieng … an” is anfangen (modern fing an) with its particle at the end, and “was soll ich anfangen” means “what am I to do.” “ich weiß mich nicht … zu finden” is an older reflexive turn — literally “I do not know myself to find out” — for not being able to find one’s way. “verhungern” is to die of hunger, not merely to be hungry.

sentences.t: Es gieng herum, suchte einen Weg, konnte aber keinen finden.
sentences.l: She went about, looked for a path, but could find none.
sentences.n: “gieng” is the 1857 spelling of ging (gehen); the ie for i runs through this whole edition. Three clauses share one subject, which German names only once.

sentences.t: Als es Abend war, setzte es sich unter einen Baum, befahl sich Gott, und wollte da sitzen bleiben und nicht weggehen, möchte geschehen was immer wollte.
sentences.l: When it was evening, she set herself down under a tree, commended herself to God, and wanted to stay sitting there and not go away, might happen what ever would.
sentences.i: When evening came she sat down under a tree, commended herself to God, and meant to stay sitting there and not go away, whatever might happen.
sentences.n: “sich Gott befehlen” is the old phrase for committing oneself to God’s keeping. “möchte geschehen was immer wollte” puts both verbs first in the subjunctive — a concessive turn: let happen what would.

sentences.t: Als es aber eine Weile da gesessen hatte, kam ein weiß Täubchen zu ihm geflogen und hatte ein kleines goldenes Schlüsselchen im Schnabel.
sentences.l: But when she had sat there a while, a little white dove came flying to her and had a small golden little key in its beak.
sentences.i: But when she had sat there a while, a little white dove came flying to her with a small golden key in its beak.
sentences.n: “ein weiß Täubchen” — the adjective stands uninflected, an older licence for “weißes.” “kam … geflogen” is the come-plus-participle pattern German uses for something approaching. The diminutives begin here and keep coming (Täubchen, Schlüsselchen, Schüsselchen, Bettchen): they carry tenderness, not only smallness.

sentences.t: Das Schlüsselchen legte es ihm in die Hand und sprach „siehst du dort den großen Baum, daran ist ein kleines Schloß, das schließ mit dem Schlüsselchen auf, so wirst du Speise genug finden und keinen Hunger mehr leiden.“
sentences.l: The little key it laid in her hand and spoke “do you see there the great tree, on it is a small lock; open that with the little key, and you will find food enough and suffer hunger no more.”
sentences.i: The little key the dove laid in her hand, and said: “Do you see that great tree yonder? There is a small lock on it; open it with the little key, and you will find food enough and go hungry no longer.”
sentences.n: The object comes first — “Das Schlüsselchen legte es …” — which is how German ties a sentence to what went before. Here “es” is the dove and “ihm” the girl, both neuter, so only the sense tells them apart. “Schloß” is the lock on the tree (the same word also means a castle); it is opened with aufschließen, particle auf at the end.

sentences.t: Da gieng es zu dem Baum und schloß ihn auf und fand Milch in einem kleinen Schüsselchen und Weißbrot zum Einbrocken dabei, daß es sich satt essen konnte.
sentences.l: Then she went to the tree and unlocked it and found milk in a small little bowl and white bread to crumble in with it, so that she could eat herself full.
sentences.i: Then she went to the tree, opened it, and found milk in a little bowl, and white bread to crumble into it, so that she could eat her fill.
sentences.n: “einbrocken” is to break bread into milk or soup, the ordinary way of taking both at once. “sich satt essen” — to eat oneself full; German makes the state of being satisfied part of the verb phrase. Weißbrot, wheaten bread, is a luxury beside everyday rye.

sentences.t: Als es satt war, sprach es „jetzt ist es Zeit, wo die Hühner daheim auffliegen, ich bin so müde, könnt ich mich doch auch in mein Bett legen.“
sentences.l: When she was full, she spoke “now it is the time when the hens fly up at home, I am so tired, if only I could lay myself in my bed too.”
sentences.i: When she had eaten her fill she said: “Now it is the hour when the hens go up to roost at home; I am so tired — if only I could lie down in my bed as well.”
sentences.n: The hens flying up to their perch at dusk tell the time as a clock would. “könnt ich mich doch” is a wish in the subjunctive with no “wenn” — if only I could; the doch carries the longing.

sentences.t: Da kam das Täubchen wieder geflogen und brachte ein anderes goldenes Schlüsselchen im Schnabel und sagte „schließ dort den Baum auf, so wirst du ein Bett finden.“
sentences.l: Then the little dove came flying again and brought another golden little key in its beak and said “unlock the tree there, and you will find a bed.”
sentences.i: Then the dove came flying again with another golden key in its beak and said: “Open that tree there, and you will find a bed.”
sentences.n: “so wirst du …” — the so after a command marks what follows from it: do this, and then that.

sentences.t: Da schloß es auf und fand ein schönes weiches Bettchen:
sentences.l: Then she unlocked it and found a beautiful soft little bed:
sentences.n: The colon does the work of “and so.” The 1857 punctuation strings events together where modern German would set a full stop.

sentences.t: da betete es zum lieben Gott, er möchte es behüten in der Nacht, legte sich und schlief ein.
sentences.l: then she prayed to the dear God, he might guard her in the night, laid herself down and fell asleep.
sentences.i: then she prayed to dear God that he would keep her through the night, lay down, and fell asleep.
sentences.n: “er möchte es behüten” is reported prayer in the subjunctive, with no “daß” needed to introduce it. “einschlafen” — to fall asleep, particle ein at the end.

sentences.t: Am Morgen kam das Täubchen zum drittenmal, brachte wieder ein Schlüsselchen und sprach „schließ dort den Baum auf, da wirst du Kleider finden,“
sentences.l: In the morning the little dove came for the third time, brought again a little key and spoke “unlock the tree there, then you will find clothes,”
sentences.i: In the morning the dove came a third time, brought another little key, and said: “Open that tree there, and you will find clothes,”
sentences.n: Threefold repetition — food, bed, clothing — is the shape these tales like, and the wording shifts only a little each time.

sentences.t: und wie es aufschloß, fand es Kleider mit Gold und Edelsteinen besetzt, so herrlich, wie sie keine Königstochter hat.
sentences.l: and when she unlocked it, she found clothes set with gold and precious stones, so splendid as no king’s-daughter has.
sentences.i: and when she opened it she found clothes set with gold and jewels, so splendid that no king’s daughter has their like.
sentences.n: “besetzt” — sewn or studded over with. The comparison stands in the present tense (“hat”), as though the teller were pointing at the world outside the tale.

sentences.t: Also lebte es da eine Zeit lang und kam das Täubchen alle Tage und sorgte für alles, was es bedurfte, und war das ein stilles, gutes Leben.
sentences.l: So she lived there a time long, and the little dove came every day and cared for everything that she needed, and that was a quiet, good life.
sentences.i: So she lived there for a time, and the dove came every day and provided everything she needed, and it was a quiet, good life.
sentences.n: “also” means “so, in this way” — a false friend for English “also,” and worth holding on to. In the clauses that follow, the verb comes first (“kam das Täubchen,” “war das”), carrying that “so” forward.

sentences.t: Einmal aber kam das Täubchen und sprach „willst du mir etwas zu Liebe thun?“
sentences.l: But once the little dove came and spoke “will you do something for love of me?”
sentences.i: But one day the dove came and said: “Will you do something for my sake?”
sentences.n: “einem etwas zu Liebe thun” is to do a thing as a kindness to someone. “thun” is the 1857 spelling of tun.

sentences.t: „Von Herzen gerne“ sagte das Mädchen.
sentences.l: “From the heart gladly,” said the girl.
sentences.i: “With all my heart,” said the girl.
sentences.n: “von Herzen gerne” is a set phrase of willing assent, unchanged in modern German.

sentences.t: Da sprach das Täubchen „ich will dich zu einem kleinen Häuschen führen, da geh hinein, mittendrein am Herd wird eine alte Frau sitzen und „guten Tag“ sagen.
sentences.l: Then the little dove spoke “I will lead you to a small little house; go in there, right in the middle at the hearth an old woman will be sitting and say “good day.”
sentences.i: Then the dove said: “I will lead you to a little house; go inside, and right in the middle, at the hearth, an old woman will be sitting, and she will say ‘good day.’
sentences.n: “mittendrein” — right into the middle of it, the older form of mittendrin. The 1857 text sets the old woman’s greeting inside the dove’s speech with the same quotation marks and no further mark; printers of the day did not distinguish an inner quotation, and the reader was left to hear it.

sentences.t: Aber gieb ihr bei Leibe keine Antwort sie mag auch anfangen, was sie will,
sentences.l: But give her on your life no answer, let her begin what she will,
sentences.i: But on no account give her any answer, whatever she may start saying,
sentences.n: “bei Leibe” — literally “by your body,” an old oath used to stiffen a prohibition: on no account. “sie mag auch anfangen, was sie will” is concessive: no matter what she begins.

sentences.t: sondern geh zu ihrer rechten Hand weiter, da ist eine Thüre, die mach auf, so wirst du in eine Stube kommen, wo eine Menge von Ringen allerlei Art auf dem Tisch liegt,
sentences.l: but go on further to her right hand, there is a door, open that, and you will come into a room where a quantity of rings of all sorts lies on the table,
sentences.i: but go on past her to her right hand; there is a door there — open it, and you will come into a room where a great many rings of every kind lie on the table,
sentences.n: “die mach auf” — the demonstrative die points back at the door and stands first, then the imperative: a very spoken word order. “Thüre” is the 1857 spelling of Türe.

sentences.t: darunter sind prächtige mit glitzerigen Steinen, die laß aber liegen und suche einen schlichten heraus, der auch darunter sein muß, und bring ihn zu mir her, so geschwind du kannst.“
sentences.l: among them are splendid ones with glittering stones, but let those lie and seek out a plain one, which must be among them too, and bring it here to me, as quickly as you can.”
sentences.i: among them are splendid ones with glittering stones; but let those lie, and pick out a plain one, which must be there among them, and bring it to me as fast as you can.”
sentences.n: “heraussuchen” — to search out, to pick from among, with heraus at the end. The plain ring is the hinge of the whole tale, and the dove says so without saying why.

sentences.t: Das Mädchen gieng zu dem Häuschen und trat zu der Thüre ein:
sentences.l: The girl went to the little house and stepped in at the door:
sentences.n: “eintreten” — to step in, the particle ein landing at the end, with “zu der Thüre” telling by which way.

sentences.t: da saß eine Alte, die machte große Augen wie sie es erblickte und sprach „guten Tag mein Kind.“
sentences.l: there sat an old woman, she made great eyes when she caught sight of her and spoke “good day, my child.”
sentences.i: there sat an old woman, who made great eyes when she caught sight of the girl, and said: “Good day, my child.”
sentences.n: “große Augen machen” is to stare in astonishment, and is still said. “die Alte” — the adjective standing as a noun, “the old one”; it is this tale’s name for the witch, and its title.

sentences.t: Es gab ihr aber keine Antwort und gieng auf die Thüre zu.
sentences.l: But she gave her no answer and went toward the door.
sentences.n: “auf etwas zugehen” — to go up to, to make for something; the particle zu at the end holds the direction.

sentences.t: „Wo hinaus?“ rief sie und faßte es beim Rock und wollte es festhalten, „das ist mein Haus, da darf niemand herein, wenn ichs nicht haben will.“
sentences.l: “Where out to?” she cried and seized her by the skirt and wanted to hold her fast, “this is my house, no one may come in here if I do not want it.”
sentences.i: “Where are you off to?” she cried, catching her by the skirt and trying to hold her fast; “this is my house, and no one may come in unless I will it.”
sentences.n: “wo hinaus?” has no verb at all — a barked question, “where away?” In “beim Rock fassen” German puts the person in the dative and the garment under a plain article where English uses a possessive; a Rock on a girl is a skirt. “ichs” = ich es.

sentences.t: Aber das Mädchen schwieg still, machte sich von ihr los und gieng gerade in die Stube hinein.
sentences.l: But the girl kept still silent, made herself loose from her and went straight into the room.
sentences.i: But the girl held her tongue, pulled free of her, and went straight into the room.
sentences.n: “sich losmachen” — to get oneself free. “schweigen” already means to be silent, and “still” only strengthens it.

sentences.t: Da lag nun auf dem Tisch eine übergroße Menge von Ringen, die glitzten und glimmerten ihm vor den Augen:
sentences.l: There now lay on the table an over-great quantity of rings, they glittered and glimmered before her eyes:
sentences.i: Now on the table lay a vast quantity of rings, and they glittered and gleamed before her eyes:
sentences.n: “ihm” is the girl once more, neuter after Mädchen. “glitzten und glimmerten” is a sound-pair, the near-rhyming doubling these tales use for dazzle.

sentences.t: es warf sie herum und suchte nach dem schlichten, konnte ihn aber nicht finden.
sentences.l: she threw them about and searched for the plain one, but could not find it.
sentences.n: “der schlichte” — the adjective standing alone as a noun, “the plain one”; German does this wherever the noun is obvious from what came before.

sentences.t: Wie es so suchte, sah es die Alte, wie sie daher schlich und einen Vogelkäfig in der Hand hatte und damit fort wollte.
sentences.l: As she was searching so, she saw the old woman, how she came creeping along and had a birdcage in her hand and wanted away with it.
sentences.i: As she was searching, she saw the old woman come creeping along with a birdcage in her hand, meaning to slip away with it.
sentences.n: German often follows a verb of seeing with a wie-clause — “sah es die Alte, wie sie …” — where English uses a bare infinitive: saw her come. “wollte fort”: the verb of motion is simply left out after wollen.

sentences.t: Da gieng es auf sie zu und nahm ihr den Käfig aus der Hand,
sentences.l: Then she went up to her and took the cage out of her hand,
sentences.n: “nahm ihr den Käfig aus der Hand” — the dative ihr says whose hand it is, which German prefers to a possessive.

sentences.t: und wie es ihn aufhob und hinein sah, saß ein Vogel darin, der hatte den schlichten Ring im Schnabel.
sentences.l: and when she lifted it up and looked inside, a bird sat in it, it had the plain ring in its beak.
sentences.i: and when she lifted it up and looked in, there sat a bird inside, and it had the plain ring in its beak.
sentences.n: “der hatte” — the demonstrative again where English would put “which”; the German simply keeps going in short strung clauses.

sentences.t: Da nahm es den Ring und lief ganz froh damit zum Haus hinaus und dachte das weiße Täubchen würde kommen und den Ring holen, aber es kam nicht.
sentences.l: Then she took the ring and ran quite glad with it out of the house and thought the white dove would come and fetch the ring, but it did not come.
sentences.i: Then she took the ring and ran out of the house with it, full of gladness, thinking the white dove would come and fetch the ring; but it did not come.
sentences.n: “zum Haus hinaus” — the pair zu … hinaus marks motion out through a thing. “würde kommen” is the subjunctive of reported thought.

sentences.t: Da lehnte es sich an einen Baum und wollte auf das Täubchen warten,
sentences.l: Then she leaned herself against a tree and wanted to wait for the little dove,
sentences.i: Then she leaned against a tree, meaning to wait for the dove,
sentences.n: “auf jemanden warten” — German waits “on” a person where English waits “for” one.

sentences.t: und wie es so stand, da war es als wäre der Baum weich und biegsam und senkte seine Zweige herab.
sentences.l: and as she stood so, it was as if the tree were soft and pliant and lowered its branches down.
sentences.i: and as she stood there, it was as though the tree were soft and pliant, and it lowered its branches.
sentences.n: “als wäre” is the subjunctive of comparison — as if it were — with no “ob” and the verb first. “herabsenken,” to sink down, particle herab last.

sentences.t: Und auf einmal schlangen sich die Zweige um es herum, und waren zwei Arme,
sentences.l: And all at once the branches wound themselves round about her, and were two arms,
sentences.i: And all at once the branches wound themselves around her, and they were two arms,
sentences.n: “schlangen” is the past of schlingen, to wind or twine — not die Schlangen, snakes. The pair um … herum encloses what is wound about. The transformation is told flatly, in the same breath as the movement, which is how these tales handle magic.

sentences.t: und wie es sich umsah, war der Baum ein schöner Mann, der es umfaßte und herzlich küßte und sagte „du hast mich erlöst und aus der Gewalt der Alten befreit, die eine böse Hexe ist.
sentences.l: and when she looked round, the tree was a handsome man, who embraced her and kissed her heartily and said “you have redeemed me and freed me from the power of the old woman, who is a wicked witch.
sentences.i: and when she looked round, the tree was a handsome man, who put his arms about her and kissed her warmly and said: “You have delivered me and freed me from the power of the old woman, who is a wicked witch.
sentences.n: “erlösen” is the tales’ word for breaking an enchantment — to redeem, to release — and it keeps a religious colouring that “rescue” has not.

sentences.t: Sie hatte mich in einen Baum verwandelt, und alle Tage ein paar Stunden war ich eine weiße Taube, und so lang sie den Ring besaß, konnte ich meine menschliche Gestalt nicht wieder erhalten.“
sentences.l: She had changed me into a tree, and every day a few hours I was a white dove, and as long as she possessed the ring, I could not get my human shape back again.”
sentences.i: She had changed me into a tree, and for a few hours every day I was a white dove; and as long as she had the ring, I could not get my human form back.”
sentences.n: “alle Tage” means every day, not “all days.” “Gestalt” is the shape a being wears, the standard word in tales of transformation.

sentences.t: Da waren auch seine Bedienten und Pferde von dem Zauber frei, die sie auch in Bäume verwandelt hatte, und standen neben ihm.
sentences.l: Then his servants and horses too were free from the spell, whom she had likewise changed into trees, and stood beside him.
sentences.i: Then his servants and horses too were freed from the spell — she had changed them into trees as well — and they stood beside him.
sentences.n: The relative clause “die sie … verwandelt hatte” is pushed to the very end, far from the servants and horses it belongs to. German bears the distance; English usually will not, so the idiomatic line breaks it out.

sentences.t: Da fuhren sie fort in sein Reich, denn er war eines Königs Sohn, und sie heiratheten sich und lebten glücklich.
sentences.l: Then they drove away into his kingdom, for he was a king’s son, and they married each other and lived happily.
sentences.i: Then they drove away to his kingdom, for he was a king’s son, and they were married and lived happily.
sentences.n: “eines Königs Sohn” — the genitive before its noun, an elevated order. “heiratheten” is the 1857 spelling of heirateten; “sich heirathen,” with the reciprocal sich, is older usage for marrying one another.

glossary.alte: die Alte — the old woman (adjectival noun; here the witch of the title); also alt — old (adj., infl.)
glossary.alten: die Alte — the old woman (adjectival noun, gen./dat.; here the witch); also alt — old (adj., infl.)
glossary.arme: der Arm — arms (nom./acc. pl.); also arm — poor (adj., infl.)
glossary.bring: bringen — bring (imperative sg.; here ‘bring … her’ = herbringen, bring here)
glossary.erhalten: erhalten — to get, obtain (infinitive; ‘wieder erhalten’ = to get back)
glossary.fuhr: fahren — travelled, drove (3rd sg. past; here of travelling by carriage)
glossary.fuhren: fahren — drove away, set off (3rd pl. past; here “fuhren fort” = fortfahren)
glossary.gerade: gerade — straight, straight in (‘gieng gerade … hinein’ = went straight in); also just, exactly
glossary.könnt: können — könnte, could (1st sg. past subjunctive, clipped; ‘könnt ich doch’ = if only I could)
glossary.liebe: die Liebe — love (‘einem etwas zu Liebe thun’ = to do a thing as a kindness to someone); also liebe — dear (lieb, infl.)
glossary.pferde: das Pferd — horses (nom./acc. pl.); also dat. sg., dem Pferde
glossary.rock: der Rock — skirt, dress (of a woman; of a man, a coat)
glossary.schlangen: schlingen — wound, twined (3rd pl. past; “schlangen sich um” = wound themselves around; not die Schlangen, snakes)
glossary.schließ: schließen — open, unlock (imperative sg.; here “schließ … auf” = aufschließen)
glossary.schloß: das Schloß — lock (here the little lock on the tree; the same word also means a castle); also schloß = schließen, shut or opened (3rd sg. past)
glossary.suche: suchen — seek out, pick out (imperative sg.; here “suche … heraus” = heraussuchen)
glossary.weg: der Weg — way, path (acc. sg.; ‘suchte einen Weg’ = looked for a path); also weg — away
glossary.weiß: weiß — white (adj.); also weiß — (I) know (wissen, 1st sg.)
glossary.wo: wo — where; also when, of a point in time (‘die Zeit, wo …’ = the time when)
